{{Short description|Measure of goodness of fit for a statistical model}}
{{distinguish|Deviate (statistics)|Deviation (statistics)|discrepancy (disambiguation)#Statistics{{!}}Discrepancy (statistics)|Divergence (statistics)}}

In [[statistics]], '''deviance''' is a [[Goodness of fit|goodness-of-fit]] statistic for a [[statistical model]]; it is often used for [[statistical hypothesis testing]]. It is a generalization of the idea of using the [[sum of squares of residuals]] (SSR) in [[ordinary least squares]] to cases where model-fitting is achieved by [[maximum likelihood]]. It plays an important role in [[exponential dispersion model]]s and [[generalized linear model]]s.

Deviance can be related to [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]].<ref>Hastie, Trevor. "A closer look at the deviance." The American Statistician 41.1 (1987): 16-20.</ref>

==Definition==
The unit deviance<ref name=J1997>{{cite book | last=Jørgensen | first = B. | year=1997 | title = The Theory of Dispersion Models | publisher = Chapman & Hall}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last=Song | first = Peter X.-K. | year=2007 | title=Correlated Data Analysis: Modeling, Analytics, and Applications | publisher=Springer Series in Statistics | doi=10.1007/978-0-387-71393-9| series = Springer Series in Statistics | isbn = 978-0-387-71392-2 }}</ref> <math>d(y,\mu)</math> is a bivariate function that satisfies the following conditions:
* <math>d(y,y) = 0</math>
* <math>d(y,\mu) > 0 \quad\forall y \neq \mu</math>
The total deviance <math>D(\mathbf{y},\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})</math> of a model with predictions <math>\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}</math> of the observation <math>\mathbf{y}</math> is the sum of its unit deviances: <math display="inline">D(\mathbf{y},\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}) = \sum_i d(y_i, \hat{\mu}_i)</math>.

The (total) deviance for a model ''M''<sub>0</sub> with estimates <math>\hat{\mu} = E[Y|\hat{\theta}_0]</math>, based on a dataset ''y'', may be constructed by its likelihood as:<ref>{{cite journal | last1= Nelder | first1 = J.A. |author-link = John Nelder | first2 = R.W.M. |last2 = Wedderburn | s2cid = 14154576 |author-link2 = Robert Wedderburn (statistician) | title = Generalized Linear Models | year=1972 | journal = Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series A (General) | volume= 135 |issue=3 | pages=370–384 | doi= 10.2307/2344614 | jstor= 2344614 }}</ref><ref name=McN>McCullagh and Nelder (1989): page 17</ref>
<math display="block">D(y,\hat{\mu}) = 2 \left(\log \left[p(y\mid\hat \theta_s)\right] - \log \left[ p(y\mid\hat \theta_0)\right]\right).</math>

Here <math>\hat \theta_0</math> denotes the fitted values of the parameters in the model ''M''<sub>0</sub>, while <math>\hat \theta_s</math> denotes the fitted parameters for the ''saturated model'': both sets of fitted values are implicitly functions of the observations ''y''. Here, the '''saturated model''' is a model with a parameter for every observation so that the data are fitted exactly. This expression is simply 2 times the [[likelihood function|log-likelihood ratio]] of the full model compared to the reduced model. The deviance is used to compare two models &ndash; in particular in the case of [[generalized linear model]]s (GLM) where it has a similar role to residual sum of squares from [[ANOVA]] in linear models ([[Residual sum of squares|RSS]]).

Suppose in the framework of the GLM, we have two [[Statistical model#Nested models|nested models]], ''M<sub>1</sub>'' and ''M<sub>2</sub>''. In particular, suppose that ''M<sub>1</sub>'' contains the parameters in ''M<sub>2</sub>'', and ''k'' additional parameters. Then, under the null hypothesis that ''M<sub>2</sub>'' is the true model, the difference between the deviances for the two models follows, based on [[Wilks' theorem]], an approximate [[chi-squared distribution]] with ''k''-degrees of freedom.<ref name=McN/> This can be used for hypothesis testing on the deviance.

Some usage of the term "deviance" can be confusing.  According to Collett:<ref>Collett (2003): page 76</ref>
: "the quantity <math>-2 \log \big[ p(y\mid\hat \theta_0)\big] </math> is sometimes referred to as a ''deviance''.  This is [...] inappropriate, since unlike the deviance used in the context of generalized linear modelling, <math>-2 \log \big[ p(y\mid\hat \theta_0)\big]</math> does not measure deviation from a model that is a perfect fit to the data." 

However, since the principal use is in the form of the difference of the deviances of two models, this confusion in definition is usually unimportant.

==Examples==
The unit deviance for the [[Poisson distribution]] is <math>d(y,\mu) = 2\left(y\log\frac{y}{\mu}-y+\mu\right)</math>, the unit deviance for the [[normal distribution]] with unit variance is given by <math>d(y,\mu) = \left(y-\mu\right)^2</math>.
